extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, IP policymakers, legal scholars and students interested in US §101/subject-matter law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether a claimed process/method (including business methods and software-related claims) constitutes patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, based on the Supreme Court's Bilski v. Kappos decision and discussion of prior tests. Useful for examiners, attorneys and policymakers evaluating/process-drafting strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (Federal Circuit formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit ruled that a claimed process is patent-eligible under §101 only if (1) it is tied to a particular machine or apparatus, or (2) it transforms a particular article into a different state or thing — and treated this 'machine-or-transformation' test as the sole applicable test for process patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the Federal Circuit's rule being reviewed; the Supreme Court rejected making this the sole and sufficient test. Use with caution and note it was repudiated as exclusive, though historically important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (Supreme Court guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held the machine-or-transformation test 'could not be a sufficient or sole test' for patent eligibility of processes, especially in the Information Age, but said the test remains 'an important and useful clue' in the §101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the machine-or-transformation test as one important indicator among others. The Court did not further define what counts as a sufficient 'transformation' or a qualifying 'particular machine', leaving those elements open to case-specific interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are 'abstract ideas' — e.g., an abstract strategy for hedging and investment — are not patentable subject matter under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed invention is mainly an abstract strategy or idea (as the Court found Bilski's claims to be), it should be excluded from patentability. Look for whether the claim adds practical application or merely recites an abstract concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods are not categorically excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court rejected a categorical exemption of business methods from patentable subject matter; the statute and precedent do not support blanket exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business-method claims can be patentable, but remain subject to the abstract-idea exclusion and other patentability requirements. Do not assume all business methods are per se unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'process' (§100(b)) governs
rubrics_metrics.description: §100(b) defines 'process' as 'process, art or method' and includes a new use of a known process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or material; the Court held that the doctrine of noscitur a sociis should not be used to narrow this statutory definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a claim is a 'process', rely on the statutory definition in §100(b) rather than attempting to narrow the meaning by association with neighboring words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statutory context (e.g., §273) to inform patent-eligibility conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court pointed to statutory provisions (such as §273(b)(1) allowing a prior-use defense for methods) as evidence that business-method patents are contemplated by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider related statutory provisions (like §273) when evaluating whether a category of claims (e.g., business methods) fits within patentable subject matter; note legislative amendments may affect interpretation (the summary notes §273 was later amended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility under §101 is only a threshold test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court reaffirmed that §101 is 'only a threshold test' for patentability: even if a claim passes §101, it still must satisfy other statutory requirements such as novelty (§102), non-obviousness (§103) and the written-description/enabling requirements (§112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stop analysis at §101. A claim that is subject-matter eligible can still be invalid for lack of novelty, obviousness, or insufficient disclosure. Use a full statutory assessment after the §101 inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty regarding what constitutes 'transformation' or 'particular machine'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court left open what exactly constitutes a 'transformation' or the requisite connection to a 'particular machine or apparatus' for §101 purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect interpretive uncertainty when applying these concepts to software, diagnostics, data-processing, and other information-age inventions; treat the machine-or-transformation factors as contextual clues rather than bright-line rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-sensitive, flexible inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court observed that 'new technologies may call for new inquiries' and that reliance on an Industrial Age test could create uncertainty for software, diagnostic techniques, data compression, and digital signal manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a flexible, technology-sensitive approach when assessing subject matter eligibility — be prepared to develop (or seek) tailored inquiries appropriate to emerging technologies rather than mechanically applying old tests.
